question.:question/problem:
The vectors $\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2},\mathbf{a}_{3}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2},\mathbf{a}_{3}\}$. In the affirmative case, find $x_{1}\cdot x_{2}\cdot x_{3}$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{b}=x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}+x_{3}\mathbf{a}_{3}$.
$\mathbf{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -5 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
By the definition of span, $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2},\mathbf{a}_{3}\}$ exactly when coefficients exist such that

$$
x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}+x_{3}\mathbf{a}_{3}=\mathbf{b}.
$$

Equating components gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x_{2}+x_{3} &= 6 \\ 2x_{1}-x_{2}-x_{3} &= -5 \\ 6x_{1}+2x_{2} &= 9\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix and use elementary row operations:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 & -5 \\ 6 & 2 & 0 & 9\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{1}\leftrightarrow R_{2}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -1 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 6 & 2 & 0 & 9\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(3\right)R_{1}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -1 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 5 & 3 & 24\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(5\right)R_{2}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -1 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & -6\end{array}\right]
$$

Back-substitution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x_{3} &= \frac{-6}{-2} = 3 \\ x_{2} &= \frac{6-\left(1\right)\left(3\right)}{1} = 3 \\ x_{1} &= \frac{-5-\left(-1\right)\left(3\right)-\left(-1\right)\left(3\right)}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All component equations hold. Thus $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2},\mathbf{a}_{3}\}$ and the coefficients are unique. Finally,

$$
x_{1}\cdot x_{2}\cdot x_{3}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\cdot \left(3\right)\cdot \left(3\right)=\frac{9}{2}.
$$

$$
x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}+x_{3}\mathbf{a}_{3}=\mathbf{b}.
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-x_{1}-x_{2}+2x_{3} &= -6 \\ -x_{1}-2x_{2}+2x_{3} &= -7 \\ x_{1}+2x_{2} &= 6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix and use elementary row operations:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-1 & -1 & 2 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & 2 & -7 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{2}\leftarrow R_{2}-\left(1\right)R_{1}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-1 & -1 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(-1\right)R_{1}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-1 & -1 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(-1\right)R_{2}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-1 & -1 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x_{3} &= \frac{-1}{2} = -\frac{1}{2} \\ x_{2} &= \frac{-1}{-1} = 1 \\ x_{1} &= \frac{-6-\left(-1\right)\left(1\right)-\left(2\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{-1} = 4\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Determine whether $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}&=\langle 0, 3, 1\rangle \\ \mathbf{c}&=\langle 1, -3, 0\rangle \\ \mathbf{u}&=\langle 2, -15, -3\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

If it does, select the value of $s\cdot t$ in $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$. Otherwise, select the statement that $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$.

Use the component equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}t &=2 \\ 3s-3t &=-15 \\ s &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

**Check all three coordinates.** Use the equations that isolate the coefficients, then verify the remaining equation.
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in\Pi$ exactly when the same values of $s$ and $t$ satisfy all three coordinate equations. Expanding the vector equation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}t &=2 \\ 3s-3t &=-15 \\ s &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 & -15 \\ 1 & 0 & -3\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-(1)R_2$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}3 & -3 & -15 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row is $0=0$, so it adds no restriction. Back substitute in the two nonzero rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{2}{1}=2 \\ s&=\frac{-15-(-3)(2)}{3}=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Verify every coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)(0)+(2)(1)&=2=2 \\ (-3)(3)+(2)(-3)&=-15=-15 \\ (-3)(1)+(2)(0)&=-3=-3\end{aligned}
$$

All three coordinates agree, so the vector lies on the plane. Therefore,

$$
s\cdot t=(-3)\cdot(2)=-6.
$$

$$

$$

Form the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 1 & 6 \\ -1 & 2 & 9 \\ -2 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_1\leftarrow (-1)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & -6 \\ -1 & 2 & 9 \\ -2 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2\leftarrow R_2-(-1)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ -2 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

question.:question/problem:

Both matrices are triangular. Multiply their main diagonal entries:

$$
\begin{aligned}\det(A)&=1\cdot(-3)\cdot2=-6,\\\det(B)&=(-2)\cdot(-1)\cdot2=4.\end{aligned}

$$

Use a Laplace expansion along row 3, then evaluate the triangular minor.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $D=\det(A)$.

Expand $D$ along row 3; only 1 nonzero entry contributes.

$$
D=(-2)(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{vmatrix}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}D_{1} &=\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\ &=(1)\cdot(2)\cdot(-3) \\ &=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these minor values,

$$
\begin{aligned}D &=(-2)(-1)^{3+3}(-6) \\ &=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\det(A)=12$.

question.:question/problem:
Let $K$ be a square matrix with $\det(K^T)=-2$, and let $I$ be the identity matrix of the same size.

Recall that transposing a matrix leaves its determinant unchanged and that $\det(I)=1$.

Which of the following statements are true? Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Transposition preserves the determinant, and the identity matrix has determinant $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\det(K^T)&=\det(K)=-2 \\ \det(I)&=1.\end{aligned}
$$

For $\det(K)=-2$,

$$
\det(K)=(-2)=-2.
$$

This statement is **true**.

For $\det(I)=0$,

$$
\det(I)=(1)=1\ne 0.
$$

This statement is **false**.

For $\det(K)+\det(I)=-1$,

$$

\det(M)=(-3)(-1)^{1+1}D_{1}+1(-1)^{1+3}D_{3}.
$$

Evaluate the minor

$$
D_{1}=\begin{vmatrix}4 & 0 & -4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 & -1\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Expand along column $2$, retaining the cofactor signs.

$$
D_{1}=(-3)(-1)^{3+2}D_{2}.
$$

Evaluate the minor

$$
D_{2}=\begin{vmatrix}4 & -4 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Use the difference of the cross products.

$$
\begin{aligned}D_{2}&=4\cdot 3-(-4)\cdot 1\\&=12-(-4)=16.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the minor

$$
D_{3}=\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 & -4 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Expand along column $1$, retaining the cofactor signs.

$$
D_{3}=1(-1)^{2+1}D_{4}.
$$

Evaluate the minor

$$
D_{4}=\begin{vmatrix}4 & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Use the difference of the cross products.

$$
\begin{aligned}D_{4}&=4\cdot (-1)-(-4)\cdot 1\\&=(-4)-(-4)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Combine the signed contributions:

$$
D_{3}=(-1)\cdot 0=0.
$$

Combine the signed contributions:

$$
D_{1}=3\cdot 16=48.

Combine the signed contributions:

$$

$$

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & -3 \\ 4 & 0 & -3 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The volume is the absolute value of its determinant:

$$
V=|\det(M)|.
$$

Expand along row $2$, retaining the cofactor signs.

$$
\det(M)=(-2)(-1)^{2+2}D_{1}+(-3)(-1)^{2+4}D_{3}.
$$

Evaluate the minor

$$
D_{1}=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & -3 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Expand along column $3$, retaining the cofactor signs.

$$
D_{1}=3(-1)^{2+3}D_{2}.
$$

Evaluate the minor

$$
D_{2}=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Use the difference of the cross products.

$$
\begin{aligned}D_{2}&=(-3)\cdot 2-1\cdot 2\\&=(-6)-2=-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the minor

$$
D_{3}=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Expand along column $2$, retaining the cofactor signs.

$$
D_{3}=1(-1)^{3+2}D_{4}.
$$

Evaluate the minor

$$
D_{4}=\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 4 & -3\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Use the difference of the cross products.

$$
\begin{aligned}D_{4}&=(-3)\cdot (-3)-1\cdot 4\\&=9-4=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Combine the signed contributions:

$$
D_{3}=(-1)\cdot 5=-5.
$$

Combine the signed contributions:

$$
D_{1}=(-3)\cdot (-8)=24.
$$

Combine the signed contributions:

$$
\det(M)=(-2)\cdot 24+(-3)\cdot (-5)=-33.
$$

Therefore,

$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}$ is a solution of $Ax=0$?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$$ A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A)&=\mathbb{R}^{5} \\ \text{rank}(A)&=5 \\ \text{Null}(A)&=\{0\} \\ \text{nullity}(A)&=0\end{aligned}\right. $$

Since $v\ne 0$ and $Av=0$, the nullspace contains a nonzero vector. Thus $A$ is not invertible. This does not determine its exact rank or nullity.

We have $\text{rank}(A)<5$, $\text{nullity}(A)>0$, $\text{Null}(A)\ne\{0\}$, and $\text{Col}(A)\ne\mathbb{R}^{5}$.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement $\text{dim(Null}(A))=0$ is false. $\text{nullity}(A)>0$.

- Statement $A\text{ is not invertible}$ is true. $A$ is not invertible.

- Statement $\text{rank}(A)<5$ is true. $\text{rank}(A)<5$; the rank counts pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is $A\text{ is not invertible}$; $\text{rank}(A)<5$ only.

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{gathered}A\text{ is invertible}\\\Updownarrow\\\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Col}(A)&=\mathbb{R}^{n}\\\dim(\operatorname{Col}(A))&=n=\operatorname{rank}(A)\\\operatorname{Null}(A)&=\{0\}\\\dim(\operatorname{Null}(A))&=0=\operatorname{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\operatorname{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^{n}$, then $A$ is invertible.* ✓

The given condition implies $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$ and $\operatorname{nullity}(A)=0$. Thus $A$ is invertible.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\operatorname{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^{n}$, then $\det(A)=0$.* ×

The given condition implies $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$ and $\operatorname{nullity}(A)=0$. Thus $\det(A)\ne 0$.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\operatorname{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^{n}$, then $\operatorname{rank}(A)<n$.* ×

The given condition implies $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$ and $\operatorname{nullity}(A)=0$. Thus $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$.

Therefore, the correct answer is I only.

BA-CA=(B-C)A.
